item.title: Sadness, Value, and Meaning
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

Sadness, Value, and Meaning

Embracing sorrow can deepen meaning and renew purpose.

Posted September 13, 2026

Key points
  • Sadness and value are opposite sides of the same coin; diminishment of one increases the other.
  • Sadness and sorrow are healing emotions when they motivate building more value in our lives.
  • When we fail to act on sadness/sorrow by blaming our losses on someone, they turn into resentment and anger.
  • When we fail to act on sadness/sorrow by dwelling on how bad they feel, they turn into depression.

The emotion of sadness occurs on a continuum from mild to intense sorrow. A natural reaction to loss, sadness/sorrow and value are opposite sides of the same coin. If we don’t feel at least a little sad at the loss of a person or thing, we didn’t value that person or thing.

To value is to hold something or someone as important, worthy of appreciation and whatever time, effort, and sacrifice may be necessary to maintain and protect.

Sadness and sorrow are healing emotions when they motivate building more value in our lives. For example, if we grieve the loss of loved ones, we will, over time, experience compassion and kindness for significant others, which will elevate self-value and deepen the meaning of our lives. To transcend sadness and sorrow, we merely need to experience them, without indulging them. Let them run their course, and they will turn into interest, compassion, and kindness.

When we fail to act on sadness/sorrow by blaming our losses on someone, they turn into resentment and anger. When we fail to act on sadness/sorrow by dwelling on how bad they feel, they turn into depression.

Depression does not improve without determined effort to create and sustain value. Medical treatment, exercise, and psychotherapy help to the extent that they facilitate value investment. Obviously, the more value we create, the harder it becomes to engage in the sort of behaviors that keep us stuck in negative moods, specifically devaluing self and others. More important, the result of creating and maintaining value revitalizes the sense of meaning and purpose.

To fight depressed mood, we must transcend present feelings. Never focus on how bad you feel or, worse, on how justified you are in feeling bad. Focus instead on what you need to do to get better. This most likely means becoming more of the person you most want to be.

How to Become the Person You Want to Be

Determine the most important things to you and what makes them important and worthy of appreciation, time, energy, and sacrifice. Next, focus on the most important qualities about you. This should lead to the core values that depressed mood is obscuring. Recommit to them, and your life will have more meaning and purpose.

Your Core Value Bank Account

You don't have to be strong in all the following areas of value investment. Make a small investment in most, with a larger investment in one or two.

  • Basic humanity (Recognizing the inherent value of other people makes us feel more humane.)
  • Love/attachment/close friendship
  • Sense of community (identification with groups of people, based on shared values, goals, or experiences)
  • Connection to nature
  • Appreciation or creation of arts, crafts, literature, music, architecture.
  • Sense of spirituality (connection to something larger than the self)
  • Compassionate behavior (helping others by supporting their capacity for autonomy and connection).

Creating value is not restricted to behavior. You can accomplish it through greater awareness of the things you already value, for example, your humanity and capacity to connect, protect, appreciate, and love. If you feel reluctant to communicate these, start by imagining them and note how you feel when you do.

item.title: Why Common Annoyances Corrode Romantic Love
item.description:
Relationships

Why Common Annoyances Corrode Romantic Love

Sweating the small stuff is crucial in marriage.

Posted September 13, 2026

Key points
  • In one survey, 33% of people listed their partner as "the most annoying person they know."
  • Annoyance with a partner is seen as an inevitable and insignificant part of living together.
  • Annoyance can hijack our attention and give rise to negative emotions.

We often decide we don’t like someone—a colleague, an acquaintance, an actor or influencer—simply because they "annoy" or "irritate" us. The habit someone has of flicking their hair, or sniffing or swallowing or the way they laugh, is enough for us to limit our exposure to them. As long as our irritation can be contained while contact is necessary and not leach into rudeness, no further reflection seems warranted. Our idiosyncratic responses to others guide our personal preferences and aversions to other people, just as do the subjective aesthetics of whom we find attractive—or not.

Intimate Annoyance

Annoyance with people close to us—people in our family with whom we live and sleep and eat and play—is very different. This isn’t annoyance we tend to disguise. Familiarity switches off our social filter, so we don’t mind showing our displeasure. We may also go on the attack as we proclaim, "You’re so annoying!" Such irritation hijacks our attention, making it impossible to ignore. One common pinch point is in adolescence, when the teen finds so much of what a parent does highly annoying. Just being in the same room with a parent, hearing them mutter to themselves as they cook or clean, rub their feet together as they watch TV, gasp or laugh at a story, can send a teen into a paroxysm of annoyance. Such irritation feels like profound criticism of who the parent is, though what the criticism actually is can be difficult to articulate beyond, "You are so annoying!"

Another hugely important dynamic is annoyance between couples. Romantic partners are expected to have a higher tolerance for aspects of our physicality that are normally repulsive to others—smells, nasal mucus, flatus—but in a survey of 2,000 people referenced by the British Psychological Society in 2021, one-third (33%) considered their "significant other" to be "the most annoying person they know."[1] Idiosyncratic habits that they could tolerate in others activated fever pitch irritation in a partner, perhaps because it is far more difficult to avoid them and because standards of tolerance are higher.

Misleading Advice on Managing Marital Annoyance

Advice for irritation management in marriage is often "don’t sweat the small stuff." [2] Familiarity breeds comfort but being in close proximity with others also risks irritability either because we become, as with allergies, more sensitive to annoying habits from repeated exposure over time [3] or because it seems impossible to balance our need for company versus our need to be alone.[4] One prominent theory is that over time we become particularly annoyed by the very characteristics that originally attracted us. The independence we once admired now seems like coldness, or the engagement with our feelings that was once comforting now feels like intrusion. [5] This model of marital annoyance fits some couples’ challenges, but its scope is limited.

More common are annoyances that arise from the need to negotiate life together, including joint management of time, children, meals, and finances as well as practical micro issues about how to squeeze toothpaste from a shared tube and who puts socks where. "Why are you always late?” “Why do I have to remind you to pack the children’s gym kit?” “Why do you keep forgetting to put the top back on the toothpaste?”

Annoyance, we are reminded, is inevitable. We should accept it and move on, focusing instead on the larger picture.

Measuring Small vs. Big Stuff

But small stuff all too easily gathers the force of a marital storm. Partners ruminate over daily irritants that infect the big picture and threaten the integrity of the relationship. “I get so anxious when you’re late.’” “When the children’s school things aren’t ready you inflict the mental load on me.” “I have to clean the bathroom shelf when the toothpaste oozes out.”

Explanations of annoyance do not simply mark different (potentially incompatible) temperaments. They frame resentment: “You don’t care how I feel/ease the burden of things I have to do.” Even something that seems to have no meaning, like a knife scraping the plate while your partner is eating, can be interpreted as not caring how that sound affects me—so not caring about me. And sometimes, the small sounds of a partner’s body functioning as bodies do—with breath and saliva and gurgles and farts—function as an infuriating reminder of their continued presence in our life, leaving us to wonder whether we even like them.

Many annoyances are shaped by gender. In my experience, women may be more likely to be irritated by habits that make more work for them. Socks left on the floor signal the insult, "Someone else (my partner) will put these away," and perhaps, "Domestic organization isn’t my concern," and, "I don’t have to think about your workload." Men may be more likely to be annoyed by a partner’s tardiness or messiness because these habits suggest she is not meeting their standards.

Some so-called "annoying" habits flag profound relational dissatisfaction. "You don’t listen when I talk to you about this,” or, “You freeze when I get upset." These annoyances are neither small irrational. They remind you, "This is a continuing problem in how we are together."

There are times when our partner bugs us because we are "jumpy" and particularly susceptible to finding small things annoying. Depression, too, can heighten irritability because everything feels "wrong." But unless we distinguish between transient annoyances and deep dissatisfaction, we won’t know when to shrug off the small stuff in marital annoyances and when to sweat it.

item.title: 4 Keys to Managing Endings
item.description:
Grief

4 Keys to Managing Endings

Not all endings are created equal, but all have the same challenges.

Posted September 13, 2026

Key points
  • Whatever the situation, endings can stir grief and loss, and with them often grief over older losses.
  • We automatically envelop the loss in a story that makes sense to us but can be damaging to our self-esteem.
  • The keys include acknowledging the loss, being careful about the story, and moving forward with a new chapter.
Source: Michitogo/Pixabay

Our lives are made up of endings: the end of childhood, of a marriage, a job, a dream. Some are obviously heavier and have more impact—a divorce, the loss of a parent, retirement. Others seem lighter—the friend who has seemed to fade away; the casual or serious relationship that mutually dissolved; the job layoff that was long expected. But regardless of the circumstances, the details, the cause, or the process, endings still create an emotional effect. All endings have a few things in common.

Grief and attachment

I’ve worked with many unfortunate victims of abusive relationships. While they are always relieved to have escaped their ordeal, a deeper look often reveals an underlying sense of loss. Loss isn’t only about the quality or nature of the relationship; it’s about attachment. We get attached to relationships that are familiar and bring a sense of safety or caring, even intermittently—whether it's a longstanding partner, a casual dating relationship, or even objects like clothes or books. When they’re gone, we grieve, even if it’s for minutes, hours, days, or months.

Loss stirs older losses

Losses are like roots on a tree. A breakup makes you think about other breakups. Job loss stirs feelings about other jobs. Losing your pet brings up memories of your long-gone parents. Like attachment, loss is a severed nerve that keeps pulsing long after. You find yourself drifting back into your past.

You create a story

No event in your life is ever just neutral—a simple noted event—but always comes with a story, a belief, and a larger context you create. This is where you need to be careful: you can get stuck in the rut of old stories that no longer fit and attack your self-esteem. The breakup is no longer just a relationship that was incompatible but another sign that you have some flaw that will prevent you from finding a close relationship. The job loss isn't just about a struggling company; it's about how life feels against you despite your efforts. There’s always some moral to an ending, but it is one that you create.

So, how do you better move through endings?

1. Understand the process

Your emotional and physical systems are taking a hit. It takes three days or three weeks, depending on the importance and length, to move through the shell-shock stage, where you obsess—what you could have done differently, why, and what about the future? Your mind is working overtime to connect the dots and make sense of what happened. Then you settle a bit—more weeks or months later—but you’re still fragile: unexpected old memories get stirred; you’re easily emotionally triggered by someone’s comment or an old song on the radio.

But eventually you feel yourself on more solid ground. The closing of a chapter. The loss has moved to the mental back burner.

2. Be gentle with yourself

I’ve met people, and you’ve probably known such folks as well, who respond to any disruption in their lives by simply plowing through it. It works in the short term, but if you never slow down to settle or accept the loss, it can come back to you later. The key is acknowledging the disruption in your life, however minor it may feel in the moment. Give it some mental and emotional space, however brief, rather than sweeping it under the rug.

3. Be careful of your story

Events in our lives are neutral. The arguments you had with your supervisor or partner may be, for you, more of the same that will eventually blow over, but for someone else the beginning of a firing or breakup. Events always come with baggage: a story, a context we make up, usually tied to past stories. We create a narrative about our lives around certain themes—that life always screws us over, that we’re never appreciated, that we’re a victim, or that moving forward and not dwelling on the past always works out.

When endings happen, be careful to ask whether you are continuing to feed an old story that not only doesn’t fit you but also fuels a negative sense of the world and of yourself, or whether this is an opportunity to change it—that you are not the victim, that the world is out to get you.

Easier said than done, of course. But with loss comes a small window of transition where you can step back and look at what’s happened through a different, often wider, lens.

4. Imagine the next chapter

Don’t do the forced-denial march forward, where you pretend that what’s happened didn’t happen. But be careful of getting stuck—licking your wounds too long, replaying the story that only casts you in the same role. Move forward both mentally and behaviorally. Imagine a new chapter, a new relationship, a new future you. Use this image as a guide, and strive to become that person in appearance, attitude, expectations, and even look.

Grieve, accept, and find closure about the past, but move forward.

item.title: Are There Any Benefits in Scrolling?
item.description:
Cognition

Are There Any Benefits in Scrolling?

The screen lights up, and the external world disappears.

Posted September 13, 2026

Key points
  • Most of us scroll without noticing we’re doing it.
  • The screen lights up, and the external world disappears.
  • We also scroll and stroll, and when we do, we're walking blind.
  • Sometimes headphones separate us even further from our surroundings.
Source: Gerd Altmann/Pixabay

Most of us scroll without noticing we’re doing it. Fingers and/or thumbs move, the screen lights up, and the “world” narrows to whatever appears in front of us. We also scroll and stroll — and when our eyes, brain, mind, and attention are on the screen, the objective, immutable fact is that we are also walking blind. We may as well have a mask over our eyes during this time, because the impact is the same.

Sometimes headphones add an additional private soundtrack that separates us even further from our surroundings; in this situation, we are both blind and deaf to the external world. We, of course, do not think that is the case because we are not wearing a mask; however, this is exactly what is happening.

During this process of scrolling and strolling, we have eliminated the external world from our brain, mind, and two of our senses; and choices have consequences (Drew et al., 2013; Ekelund et al., 2022; Nobre et al., 2020; Purje, 2014; Raveh & Lavie, 2015).

How Brain Plasticity Responds to Digital Immersion

Neuroscience research indicates that, because of brain plasticity, the brain is always responding, always firing, rewiring and adapting to whatever we think, do, say, learn and choose. As such, when scrolling on a cell phone or sitting at a computer becomes the dominant rhythm of daily life, the brain immediately begins to fire, rewire, and adapt to these choices and behaviors.

With scrolling, what is now taking place involves rapid visual shifts, instant novelty, and constant stimulation.

As this change happens, the brain and mind become immersed in and adept at “novelty‑driven” fragmented, microsecond presentations.

Impact on Critical Thinking and Complex Skills Development

This results in a brain and mind that do not develop the complex neurobiological connections required for critical thinking and higher‑order reasoning, nor the associated skill‑acquisition potential and knowledge that develop the brain, mind and body for the complexities of life.

This scrolling and immersive life choice influences not only how we think, but also how we feel, how we relate, and how we behave (Carr, 2010; Doidge, 2007; Graybiel, 2008; Loh & Kanai, 2016).

Education systems are now beginning to see the consequences of these technology-driven behaviors. In the State of Maine, for example, a 20-year statewide initiative costing billions of dollars introduced computers widely into classrooms in the hope and desire of improving academic performance. Instead, during those two decades, academic standards declined (Rogelberg, 2026).

Recently in Australia, national literacy and numeracy assessments have shown similar downward trends, prompting the Federal, State and Territory governments to intervene urgently.

These results do not condemn technology. They simply reveal that when digital immersion becomes the default mode of thinking, behavior, learning, and choices, the brain and mind adapt in ways that do not – as the results inform – support academic growth or thinking (ACARA, 2026).

Turning this behavioral choice around does not require a revolution. It requires self-awareness, self-discipline and agency. It requires the universal recognition and understanding that the brain changes based on what we think, do, say, learn, and choose.

If we want efficient analytical minds, healthier emotions, and more connected communities, individuals and society must make choices that support those outcomes (Purje, 2014).

The Role of Internet and AI in Personal and Collective Responsibility

The internet and the immense, unimaginable power of Artificial Intelligence (A.I.) are now a permanent part of human life. But how we engage with these tools—and how often—remains a matter of personal and collective choice and responsibility.

Each individual – and society as a collective – has the power to decide how much of their day is spent scrolling and how much is spent in the actions that involve and develop critical thinking, higher-order reasoning, and the development of associated physical skills and knowledge. I think, therefore I am (Descartes). I am what I think, do, say, learn and choose (Purje, 2014).

item.title: There Is Power in Being Grateful
item.description:
Gratitude

There Is Power in Being Grateful

Research increasingly shows that gratitude can help support the mind and body.

Posted September 13, 2026

Key points
  • Gratitude can reduce stress, depression, and burnout, especially in healthcare workers.
  • Being grateful has been linked to lower blood pressure and better heart health outcomes.
  • Expressing gratitude could improve sleep, reduce headaches, and boost self-care in nurses.

You have probably heard the phrase, "Count your blessings.” It is a saying among religious people to remind them to be thankful for what is positive and good in their life. Often this reminder helps people when they may be tending to focus on a recent negative event, or feeling depressed, and focusing on all the negative aspects of their life lately. Aside from a temporary redirection of focus away from the negative, does this thankfulness, or gratitude, produce any other psychological, emotional, or even biological changes in us? This question has been at the heart of much research in psychology and medicine for decades, and even more in the last 20 years with increased stress, political division, pandemics, and loneliness fueled by social media. What research has revealed about being grateful may surprise you.

From the early philosophers, such as Descartes, who debated the “mind-body” problem (how can thoughts influence a physical thing like the body), psychologists have been speculating about the influence of the way we think on our body. While a detailed discussion of the mind-body issue is beyond the purpose of this brief post, here are a few examples as an entrance into our discussion. In the early and mid-1900s, John Watson and B.F. Skinner (respectively) didn’t want to assume anything about thoughts or cognition since they couldn’t scientifically verify that cognition exists, so they only focused on observable behavior when they created the “behaviorism” school of thought. I’m skipping over a number of other studies, but just wanted to mention a couple more. A classic study by Langer and Rodin (1976) examined perceived control over their environment among nursing home patients (e.g., whether they can be in charge of caring for a plant in their room, or what shows to watch on TV, or other aspects of their daily life). The results showed that in those who were given more control over their environment, 93% showed overall improvement, became more active, and felt happier. Of those who were in the no control group, 71% became more debilitated in as soon as three weeks. In a meta-analysis of 15 studies encompassing 229,000 patients, Rozanski et al. (2019) examined the influence of optimism and pessimism on the likelihood of cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality. The data showed a strong effect of optimism: those who were optimistic were significantly less likely to experience cardiovascular events, and they had a significantly lower mortality rate than pessimists.

These few examples are just the tip of the iceberg. There are many studies demonstrating the powerful effects of the way we think over our physical well-being. So much so that in 1978, APA created Division 38 (Health Psychology) to formally recognize and organize this new field and its popularity (Division 38, Society for Health Psychology, 2023). I would like to now turn to the focus of this particular blog post: the influence of gratitude on mental and physical well-being.

Psychological Well-Being

Research shows that being grateful has a significant positive effect on the mental health of healthcare workers. It has been shown to reduce emotional exhaustion in mental healthcare workers (Lanham, et al., 2012; Yaqub, 2025), and reduce stress and depressive symptoms in healthcare workers (Cheng et al, 2015). Starkey et al. (2019) found that being the recipient of gratitude was also beneficial to healthcare workers (in this case, nurses). The researchers found that the more that nurses were thanked for their efforts, the more they felt a deeper satisfaction with the care they provided and they also had better sleep, fewer headaches, and they took better care of their own health. Being grateful can also be a buffer for spousal caregivers in that it can reduce anxiety and feelings of being overwhelmed, and increase psychological well-being (Nah, Martire, & Zhaoyang, 2022).

Heart Health

Gratitude, paired with optimism, has a strong benefit for cardiovascular wellness. Research by Millstein et al. (2016) with the recovery of patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) found that gratitude and optimism predicted better adherence to medical advice six months later, as well as lower anxiety and depression (see also similar findings with ACS patients by Legler et al. (2019)). Some data support the idea that gratitude is associated with lower systolic blood pressure (Gallagher et al., 2020; Ginty, et al., 2020; Leavy, et al., 2023), and better regulation of the heart rate (Schwerdtfeger et al., 2025). Ginty and colleagues (2020) posit that one explanation for this relationship between gratitude and better heart functioning is that gratitude prior to exposure to a stressor may provide a protective function for cardiovascular functioning.

Stress

Feeling grateful reduces stress and depression (Nezlek, Krejtz, Rusanowska, & Holas, 2019; Wolfe, 2021; Wood, et al, 2008). It is negatively associated with work stress (Ahrens, 2017), and work burnout (Lee, et al., 2018). Research also shows that gratitude interventions and optimism reduce suicidal ideation in sexual assault survivors (Kumar et al., 2022) and military veterans with PTSD (Kumar, et al., 2024). This remarkable positive effect of gratitude on powerful, emotional trauma like assault and war has also been shown to mitigate the intense feelings of grief. Gratitude is associated with better coping with grief (Beckley, 2023) and greater resilience and even flourishing through grief and loss (Elfers. et al., 2024). Many studies have found that gratitude is associated with lower stress among healthcare workers (Lanham, et al, 2012; Yaqub, 2025). Starkey et al. (2019) reported that the more nurses were thanked for their efforts, they felt a greater quality of sleep, satisfaction with the care they provided, decreased headaches and better care of their own health.

Summary

The research on gratitude has been increasing over the decades and has only accelerated in recent years. There is good reason, as our brief review of the recent research attests. Gratitude has powerful effects on our psychological, emotional, and physical well-being. This research suggests that often, positive changes in your mental and physical health can be accomplished by the simple act of being and feeling grateful for your life, the people in it, and the positive events, and yes, even the negative events in your life.
